paragraphs.heading: The fourth state
paragraphs.text: After solid, liquid and gas, plasma is often named the fourth state of matter. It forms when one of the other states, often a gas, has been ionized to a large degree, so that a big share of it is made of charged particles, ions and electrons. It becomes such a good conductor of electricity that long-range electric and magnetic fields control how it behaves.

paragraphs.heading: Rare here, common out there
paragraphs.text: Plasma is rarely encountered on Earth, yet an estimated 99.9% of ordinary matter in the universe is plasma. Stars are almost pure balls of it, and it dominates the thin gas between galaxies and inside galaxy clusters. Neon signs and lightning are examples closer to home. They are partially ionized plasmas, which means some neutral particles are still mixed in.

paragraphs.heading: How the charges act together
paragraphs.text: Its charged particles make plasma a conductor of electricity. Overall it is usually close to neutral: positive and negative charges in any sizeable region roughly balance, a property called quasineutrality. The particles are unbound, but they are not free of forces. Every moving charge creates currents and fields that act on the other charges and are acted on by them, so the plasma moves in collective ways and reacts strongly to fields applied from outside.

paragraphs.heading: Making and using plasma
paragraphs.text: People can make plasma, for example by heating a neutral gas or by putting it in a strong electromagnetic field. The way plasma responds to such fields is put to work in many technologies, including plasma televisions, plasma etching and efforts to develop fusion energy.

paragraphs.heading: No sharp boundary
paragraphs.text: Unlike the changes between solid, liquid and gas, the change into plasma has no clear-cut point. Whether a substance counts as plasma is a matter of interpretation and context. How much ionization is enough depends on which phenomenon is being studied.

paragraphs.heading: Where the name came from
paragraphs.text: Plasma science grew out of the history of electricity. Vasily Petrov and Humphry Davy each discovered the electric arc in 1803, and in 1831 Michael Faraday studied glowing electric discharges in thin gases. In 1879 William Crookes, who worked on low-pressure discharges, put forward the idea of a fourth state of matter. Irving Langmuir first used the word plasma in the 1920s. The way electrons were carried along reminded him of how blood plasma carries red and white blood cells and germs.

paragraphs.heading: Unusual plasmas
paragraphs.text: Some plasmas break the usual pattern. A non-neutral plasma has a large excess of one kind of charge, or is made of a single kind of particle, and electric fields dominate it; charged particle beams are one example. A dusty plasma holds tiny charged grains of dust, typically found in space, which pick up high charges and interact with each other. In the laboratory these are also called complex plasmas.
